ep-man-001.question: Narrow-QRS tachycardia, cycle length 360 ms, 1:1 A:V relationship. RV pacing at 340 ms accelerates the atria to the pacing cycle length. On cessation of pacing you read a V-A-A-V sequence. Before diagnosing atrial tachycardia, which checks are relevant? (multiple answers)
options: Make sure the first A counted is really the last A accelerated to the pacing cycle length
Require QRS fusion during pacing to validate the manoeuvre
Repeat the manoeuvre at shorter cycle lengths to show the response is reproducible
Check that the PPI − TCL exceeds 115 ms
Reassess the response using the His (A-A-H or A-H) rather than the ventricular electrogram alone
commentaires: Correct: if VA conduction is slow, the first A after the last V may result from the penultimate stimulus; the right starting point is the last A accelerated to the pacing cycle length.
Incorrect: fusion proves entrainment of AVRT but is not required to interpret a V-A-V / V-A-A-V response; it is in any case impossible in AVNRT and AT.
Correct: the first AT beat may occur by coincidence at an interval equal to the pacing cycle length; a response reproduced at decreasing cycle lengths is more robust.
Incorrect: PPI − TCL is used to distinguish AVNRT from AVRT once AT has been excluded; it does not help to establish AT.
Correct: in AVNRT with HV > HA, a tachycardia A is inscribed before the V without having been conducted from it; reasoning on the His avoids this pseudo-V-A-A-V response.
ep-man-001.explication: A V-A-A-V (A-A-H) response after ventricular pacing is the strongest argument for atrial tachycardia, because the last retrograde A cannot conduct back down to the ventricle through a conduction system that is still refractory: the next A comes from the focus. Three pitfalls produce false V-A-A-V responses. First, long VA conduction (atypical AVNRT, decremental pathway): the first A after the last V then results from the penultimate stimulus. Second, AVNRT with HV > HA: the tachycardia A follows the His and precedes the V without having been generated by it; this is why an A-H / A-A-H analysis is preferred. Third, coincidence, hence the value of repeating the manoeuvre at shorter cycle lengths. A change in atrial activation sequence between pacing (low-to-high) and tachycardia (high-to-low) strengthens the diagnosis of AT.
ep-man-001.aRetenir: Before calling a V-A-A-V response: identify the last entrained A, reason on the His (A-A-H) and check reproducibility.

ep-man-002.question: Long RP tachycardia, cycle length 380 ms, concentric atrial activation. RV pacing at 360 ms accelerates the atria; the stimulus-to-A interval is 415 ms. After the last stimulus there is an A at 55 ms, a second A at 415 ms, then the V. How should this sequence be interpreted?
options: Genuine V-A-A-V response, favouring focal atrial tachycardia
Uninterpretable response, because the VA exceeds the pacing cycle length
Pseudo-V-A-A-V: a V-A-V response, atrial tachycardia excluded
V-A-V response proving orthodromic AVRT
commentaires: Incorrect: the first A (55 ms) is the response to the penultimate stimulus (415 − 360 = 55 ms); it must not be counted.
Incorrect: the response remains interpretable once the last A accelerated to the pacing cycle length has been correctly identified.
Correct: the two As are 360 ms apart, i.e. the pacing cycle length; the second is the last entrained A, directly followed by the V: the response is V-A-V.
Incorrect: a V-A-V response excludes AT but does not distinguish atypical AVNRT from AVRT; quantitative criteria are needed (cPPI − TCL, SA − VA).
ep-man-002.explication: When the retrograde limb of the circuit conducts slowly (fast-slow or slow-slow AVNRT, slowly conducting accessory pathway), the stimulus-to-A interval may exceed the pacing cycle length. The first A inscribed after the last stimulus then comes from the penultimate one: here 415 − 360 = 55 ms. The clue to this pitfall is the interval between the two As, equal to the pacing cycle length (360 ms), and a stimulus-to-A interval identical to that measured during pacing. The last truly entrained A is therefore the second one, followed by the V: a V-A-V response, which excludes atrial tachycardia. In the case reported by Veenhuyzen, the diagnosis was fast-slow AVNRT (cPPI − TCL 185 ms, SA − VA 150 ms).
ep-man-002.aRetenir: If the VA exceeds the pacing cycle length, two consecutive As separated by the pacing cycle length indicate a pseudo-V-A-A-V response: it is in fact V-A-V.

ep-man-003.question: Narrow-QRS tachycardia with concentric activation, VA 110 ms, cycle length 360 ms. After entrainment from the RV apex at 340 ms (V-A-V response), the PPI is 480 ms. The AH is 150 ms during tachycardia and 200 ms on the first return beat. What is your diagnosis?
options: Atypical AVNRT, because the PPI − TCL exceeds 115 ms
Atrial tachycardia, because the AH lengthens on the return beat
None: a PPI − TCL of 120 ms lies in the grey zone
Septal AVRT: cPPI − TCL = 70 ms
commentaires: Incorrect: the uncorrected PPI − TCL (120 ms) is inflated by decremental AV nodal slowing; it must be corrected.
Incorrect: the V-A-V response has already excluded AT; the AH prolongation reflects decremental AV nodal conduction at a short cycle length.
Incorrect: the correction is precisely what resolves the ambiguity of the uncorrected PPI.
Correct: cPPI − TCL = (480 − 360) − (200 − 150) = 120 − 50 = 70 ms, below the 110 ms cut-off: favours a septal accessory pathway.
ep-man-003.explication: The PPI measures the time taken for the last paced wavefront to reach the circuit, travel round it and return to the pacing site: the further the site is from the circuit, the longer the PPI − TCL. However, during entrainment of AVRT the AV node receives atrial impulses at the pacing cycle length and its conduction slows (decrement): the AH of the first return beat lengthens for reasons unrelated to the distance from the circuit. The González-Torrecilla correction subtracts this prolongation: cPPI − TCL = PPI − TCL − (return AH − tachycardia AH). A cPPI − TCL < 110 ms points to AVRT using a septal pathway, > 110 ms to AVNRT. Here the uncorrected PPI wrongly suggested AVNRT. The correction also avoids the pitfall of a jump to the slow pathway on the first return beat.
ep-man-003.aRetenir: cPPI − TCL = PPI − TCL − ΔAH (return − tachycardia); cut-off 110 ms: below it, septal accessory pathway.

ep-man-004.question: In which situations can entrainment by ventricular pacing yield long values (PPI − TCL, cPPI − TCL or SA − VA) even though the tachycardia is orthodromic AVRT? (multiple answers)
options: Left lateral accessory pathway, pacing from the RV apex
Septal accessory pathway, pacing at the base close to the earliest atrial activation
Decrementally conducting accessory pathway (long RP tachycardia)
AVRT via a left lateral pathway with functional left bundle branch block
Jump to the nodal slow pathway on the first return beat, for the uncorrected PPI − TCL
commentaires: Correct: the RV apex is far from the ventricular insertion of the pathway; this extra distance lengthens the cPPI − TCL and SA − VA.
Incorrect: on the contrary, this is the situation that gives the shortest values, as the site is close to the circuit.
Correct: a decremental pathway slows at short cycle lengths; SA and PPI lengthen and may mimic atypical AVNRT.
Incorrect: with functional LBBB the RV is part of the circuit; RV pacing is then close to the circuit and the values are short.
Correct: conduction over the slow pathway during entrainment markedly lengthens the first AH, and therefore the uncorrected PPI; AH correction removes this effect.
ep-man-004.explication: The quantitative criteria of Michaud (PPI − TCL > 115 ms, SA − VA > 85 ms) and González-Torrecilla (cPPI − TCL > 110 ms) were validated to distinguish atypical AVNRT from a SEPTAL accessory pathway. They lose their value when the pacing site is far from the pathway, typically a left lateral pathway entrained from the RV apex: the values become "borderline" or frankly long. A decremental pathway (Coumel type, long RP) also lengthens SA and PPI. A jump to the slow pathway on the first return beat lengthens the uncorrected PPI, hence the value of AH correction. In these cases, one turns to basal pacing close to the earliest atrial activation, differential entrainment or a His-refractory PVC.
ep-man-004.aRetenir: Long PPI − TCL and SA − VA values indicate AVNRT only once a distant or decremental pathway has been ruled out.

ep-man-005.question: Tachycardia with concentric activation, VA 120 ms. Entrainment (V-A-V response) at the same cycle length from the RV apex and then the RV base (above the His, without His or atrial capture). Apex: SA − VA 95 ms, cPPI − TCL 115 ms. Base: SA − VA 130 ms, cPPI − TCL 160 ms. Conclusion?
options: Septal AVRT: the base is closer to the pathway
AVNRT: the values increase by 35 and 45 ms at the base
Atrial tachycardia: the response varies with the site
Inconclusive: different cycle lengths are needed at the two sites
commentaires: Incorrect: with a septal pathway, pacing near its insertion would shorten SA and PPI at the base, not the reverse.
Correct: differential VA (base − apex) = 35 ms (> 20) and differential cPPI − TCL = 45 ms (> 30): an AVNRT profile.
Incorrect: the V-A-V response obtained at both sites has already excluded AT; differential entrainment is used here to separate AVNRT from AVRT.
Incorrect: quite the opposite, long and IDENTICAL cycle lengths are required at both sites so that AV nodal decrement does not distort the comparison.
ep-man-005.explication: In AVNRT, the RV apex is electrically closer to the circuit than the base, because the Purkinje network is entered mainly at the apex: pacing the base forces the impulse to cross the myocardium before ascending the His, and to repeat the journey on the way back. SA and PPI therefore lengthen at the base. In AVRT, by contrast, a base close to the pathway insertion shortens these values. Segal et al. proposed "differential entrainment": a differential VA > 20 ms and a differential cPPI − TCL > 30 ms (base − apex) identify AVNRT. Advantage: there is no need to know the site of earliest atrial activation. Caveat: the cycle lengths must be identical and long enough, with no His or atrial capture at the base.
ep-man-005.aRetenir: Differential entrainment: longer values at the base than at the apex (VA +20 ms, cPPI +30 ms) = AVNRT.

ep-man-006.question: True or false: clear QRS fusion during entrainment of a narrow-QRS tachycardia by ventricular pacing (inadvertent His capture having been excluded) rules out AVNRT and atrial tachycardia.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: fusion implies collision with the tachycardia wavefront within the ventricular myocardium, hence a ventricle that is part of the circuit: this is AVRT.
Incorrect: in AVNRT and AT the collision occurs in the AV node or His; the paced QRS cannot be fused.
ep-man-006.explication: During entrainment, the antidromic paced wavefront collides with the orthodromic wavefront of the preceding beat. In AVNRT the collision occurs in the nodal slow pathway; in AT, in the conduction system: the ventricle is entirely activated by pacing and the QRS cannot be fused. In AVRT, the tachycardia wavefront exits the Purkinje network and activates part of the ventricle before the collision, so fusion is possible. Fusion therefore proves entrainment, a re-entrant mechanism and participation of the ventricle and of an accessory pathway. It is highly specific but insensitive, especially for a left-sided pathway paced from the RV. Pitfall: at the septal base, capture of the His or right bundle can produce a narrow QRS that mimics fusion.
ep-man-006.aRetenir: QRS fusion during ventricular entrainment = AVRT (specific, insensitive); impossible in AVNRT and AT.

ep-man-007.question: Probable AVRT with earliest atrial activation in the distal coronary sinus. Entrainment from the RV apex shows no fusion and gives borderline values. Where should you pace to maximise the chance of seeing fusion?
options: RV apex, at high output to capture more myocardium
RV outflow tract, far from the Purkinje network
Para-Hisian region, with His capture
LV base (coronary sinus), opposite the early A
commentaires: Incorrect: increasing the output does not bring the site closer to the circuit; the collision still occurs in the conduction system.
Incorrect: the outflow tract is still far from a left lateral pathway.
Incorrect: His capture produces a narrow QRS that mimics fusion and prevents any interpretation.
Correct: pacing close to the ventricular insertion of the pathway, far from the Purkinje exit, gives the tachycardia wavefront time to activate myocardium before the collision.
ep-man-007.explication: For fusion to be visible, the orthodromic wavefront of the preceding beat must activate as much myocardium as possible before meeting the paced wavefront. The ideal site is therefore as far as possible from the Purkinje exit while remaining close to the circuit, i.e. the ventricular base opposite the earliest atrial activation. From the RV apex, fusion is seen in most AVRTs using septal or right-sided pathways, but rarely with a left-sided pathway. From the LV (often accessible via a coronary sinus branch), it becomes visible in most left-sided pathways, sometimes as concealed fusion (QRS identical to that of the tachycardia). A basal site also reduces the cPPI − TCL and SA − VA in AVRT.
ep-man-007.aRetenir: To see fusion, pace at the base, as close as possible to the ventricular insertion of the pathway (LV via the coronary sinus for a left-sided pathway).

ep-man-008.question: Narrow-QRS tachycardia, cycle length 300 ms. RV pacing at 280 ms: the first four paced QRS complexes are fused and the 5th has the fully paced morphology. The atrial cycle is advanced from the 2nd stimulus onwards, with no change in sequence, and the SA then remains fixed. Which diagnosis does the onset of this train suggest?
options: Orthodromic AVRT
Typical slow-fast AVNRT
Atypical fast-slow AVNRT
Septal focal atrial tachycardia
commentaires: Correct: the atrium is perturbed within the transition zone, before the first stable paced QRS: the paced wavefront reaches it as soon as it engages the pathway.
Incorrect: in AVNRT the atrium is perturbed only after the transition zone, once the wavefront has travelled up the His–Purkinje system and AV node.
Incorrect: same reasoning as for typical AVNRT: late atrial perturbation, after the first stable QRS.
Incorrect: a fused QRS is His-refractory; the fact that it advances the atrium can only be explained by an accessory pathway.
ep-man-008.explication: At the onset of ventricular pacing, the QRS complexes pass through a fused transition zone before reaching a stable paced morphology (defined on all 12 leads). In AVRT, the paced wavefront reaches the atrium as soon as it encounters the pathway: atrial activation is advanced or delayed, or the tachycardia terminates, within the transition zone or at the first stable QRS. In AVNRT, the wavefront must first ascend the His–Purkinje system and AV node: the perturbation occurs after the first stable QRS. The predictive value exceeds 90% in retrospective studies. A further advantage: the criterion remains usable if the tachycardia does not resume after pacing. Limitations: inter-observer agreement of about 80% for identifying the first stable QRS, too short a pacing cycle length, bystander or decremental pathway.
ep-man-008.aRetenir: Atrium perturbed within the transition zone (fused QRS) = AVRT; after the first stable paced QRS = AVNRT.

ep-man-009.question: During a narrow-QRS tachycardia you deliver premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) and want to know whether they are "His-refractory". Which criteria establish this? (multiple answers)
options: The PVC QRS is fused with the tachycardia QRS
The PVC advances the next atrial activation
The stimulus falls just after the visible antegrade His
The PVC is delivered 100 ms before the expected His
The stimulus precedes the expected His by no more than 35–55 ms
commentaires: Correct: fusion proves that the tachycardia wavefront has already exited the Purkinje network, and therefore that the His has been activated.
Incorrect: this is the result being interpreted, not a criterion of refractoriness; the reasoning would be circular.
Correct: if the His has just been activated, it is necessarily refractory to the retrograde wavefront.
Incorrect: 100 ms earlier, the paced wavefront has time to ascend to the His before the tachycardia impulse; the PVC is no longer His-refractory.
Correct: this is the time the paced wavefront needs to reach the distal Purkinje fibres and ascend to the His; within this window, the two wavefronts meet in the His.
ep-man-009.explication: A His-refractory PVC cannot ascend through the His and AV node: any effect on the atrium (advance, delay) or any termination without atrial activation implies an accessory pathway. One must still be sure of refractoriness. There are three criteria: a fused QRS (the tachycardia wavefront has already passed through the His), a stimulus delivered just after a visible antegrade His, or a stimulus that precedes the expected His by no more than 35–55 ms. Any earlier and the PVC is not His-refractory and may modify AVNRT or AT via the node. Sensitivity increases when the PVC is delivered close to the pathway insertion, at the base. The manoeuvre is unreliable if the tachycardia cycle length varies more than the effect being measured.
ep-man-009.aRetenir: His-refractory PVC: fused QRS, stimulus after the His, or no more than 35–55 ms before the expected His.

ep-man-010.question: Long RP tachycardia, stable cycle length 473 ms, earliest atrial activation at the coronary sinus ostium. RV entrainment: cPPI − TCL 150 ms, SA − VA 120 ms. A PVC delivered when the His is expected delays the next atrial activation by 20 ms, without changing the atrial sequence. What is your diagnosis?
options: Atypical slow-slow AVNRT, based on the entrainment criteria
Septal atrial tachycardia with coincidental VA conduction
AVRT using a decremental accessory pathway
Atypical AVNRT with a bystander accessory pathway
commentaires: Incorrect: these long values are expected with a decremental pathway and are not enough to diagnose AVNRT in the face of the PVC response.
Incorrect: a His-refractory PVC cannot delay AT without an accessory pathway; the decremental V→A link is incompatible with AT.
Correct: a His-refractory PVC that delays the atrium without changing the sequence proves a decremental pathway participating in the circuit.
Incorrect: a bystander pathway might possibly advance the atrium, but a delay reflects decremental V→A coupling intrinsic to the circuit.
ep-man-010.explication: A decremental retrograde accessory pathway (Coumel type) typically causes a long RP tachycardia with posteroseptal activation. During entrainment its conduction slows at short cycle lengths: cPPI − TCL and SA − VA become long and mimic atypical AVNRT. The His-refractory PVC settles the question: as the His is refractory, a delay in the atrium can only occur via an accessory pathway, and this delay shows that atrial activation depends decrementally on ventricular activation. The pathway therefore participates in the circuit. To be visible, the slowing must exceed the prematurity of the PVC: the whole His-refractory window must be scanned. Here the PVC response takes precedence over the entrainment values.
ep-man-010.aRetenir: Long RP tachycardia: a His-refractory PVC that DELAYS the atrium indicates a participating decremental pathway, even if PPI and SA − VA are long.

ep-man-011.question: True or false: in a tachycardia resembling typical AVNRT (concentric activation, septal VA < 70 ms), scanning diastole with His-refractory PVCs does not help to distinguish AVNRT from atrial tachycardia.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: a His-refractory PVC can reach neither the nodal circuit nor the atrium in AT; it has no effect in either case. The manoeuvre of choice is ventricular entrainment.
Incorrect: a His-refractory PVC can only affect a circuit that uses an accessory pathway; it is silent in AVNRT as well as in AT.
ep-man-011.explication: A His-refractory PVC meets the tachycardia wavefront in the His–Purkinje system or the myocardium: it cannot modify AVNRT or AT, except via a bystander accessory pathway. Its role is to demonstrate an accessory pathway, particularly a septal pathway participating in the circuit. A VA < 70 ms, however, already virtually excludes orthodromic AVRT: the remaining question is AVNRT or AT, and the His-refractory PVC will be silent in both. The appropriate manoeuvre is ventricular entrainment (V-A-V versus V-A-A-V response), or observation of spontaneous variations (H-H changes that precede and predict A-A changes, termination with a non-premature A). Exception: in an "AVNRT-like" tachycardia with too short a PPI or with fusion, His-refractory PVCs may reveal a nodoventricular pathway.
ep-man-011.aRetenir: VA < 70 ms: the question is AVNRT or AT; the His-refractory PVC is silent, so perform ventricular entrainment.

ep-man-012.question: Narrow-QRS tachycardia, 1:1 A:V relationship, central atrial activation. On three attempts, RV pacing 20–30 ms faster than the tachycardia fails to accelerate the atria: the tachycardia continues, dissociated from the paced ventricles. What can be concluded?
options: AVNRT is proven, because the VA was short
AVRT is excluded; AT is likely but not proven
Atrial tachycardia is definitely proven
Nothing: the response is uninterpretable and uninformative
commentaires: Incorrect: dissociation does not prove AVNRT; AT is in fact the most frequent diagnosis in this situation.
Correct: AVRT cannot survive V-A dissociation; AT is the most frequent diagnosis, but AVNRT with retrograde block remains possible.
Incorrect: AVNRT is not excluded; further evidence is needed (atrial pacing, VA linking).
Incorrect: the V-A-V/V-A-A-V response cannot be analysed, but dissociation already excludes AVRT.
ep-man-012.explication: In 50–80% of atrial tachycardias, ventricular pacing does not accelerate the atria: the ventricles are dissociated from the mechanism. The post-pacing response then cannot be interpreted, but the information remains useful: the ventricle is not required for the tachycardia, which excludes AVRT via an accessory pathway. The diagnosis is most often AT (about 80% of cases with central activation), but AVNRT with intermittent retrograde block is not excluded. Atrial pacing (VA linking), spontaneous or adenosine-induced termination, or isoprenaline can then help. A false conclusion due to isorhythmic dissociation must also be avoided: pacing cycle length too long or tachycardia accelerating.
ep-man-012.aRetenir: Ventricular pacing that does not accelerate the atria, with persisting tachycardia: AVRT excluded, AT likely but not proven.

ep-man-013.question: True or false: when ventricular pacing accelerates the atria but terminates the tachycardia on every attempt, the manoeuvre provides no diagnostic information.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: termination prevents analysis of the post-pacing response and PPI, but other features of the drive train can still be used.
Correct: one can analyse the beat preceding VA block, measure an SA for differential entrainment, or shorten nodal refractoriness with isoprenaline.
ep-man-013.explication: If the atria follow the pacing cycle length but the tachycardia does not resume, the cycle length has often encroached on antegrade AV nodal refractoriness: the last retrograde A cannot conduct back down. Isoprenaline, by shortening nodal refractoriness, often allows the manoeuvre to be repeated. Even without resumption, termination remains informative. If the stimulus preceding VA block is His-refractory (fused QRS) and the atrium was not affected beforehand, this is equivalent to a His-refractory PVC that terminates the tachycardia without reaching the atrium: the diagnosis is AVRT. The SA measured during acceleration can also be used to calculate an apex–base differential VA. Finally, a burst of 3 to 6 stimuli at 200–250 ms often dissociates the ventricles (AVRT excluded) or terminates the tachycardia without reaching the atrium (AT excluded).
ep-man-013.aRetenir: Repeated termination during ventricular pacing: analyse the onset of the train, use the SA, try isoprenaline; the manoeuvre is still informative.

ep-man-014.question: True or false: a V-A-V (A-H) response after ventricular entrainment definitively rules out any atrial tachycardia in this patient, including after ablation of the identified circuit.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: a V-A-V response excludes AT as the mechanism of the tachycardia under study, not the coexistence of an AT.
Correct: an A-H response proves that the ongoing tachycardia is AVNRT or AVRT, but an associated AT remains possible; re-induction is required after ablation.
ep-man-014.explication: A V-A-V response means that the last retrograde wavefront was able to conduct back down to the ventricle, which is only possible if the tachycardia under study is AVNRT or AVRT. It says nothing about the existence of another substrate. Several mechanisms can coexist in the same patient: AVNRT and an accessory pathway, AVRT and AT, and so on. Good practice is to repeat a stimulation protocol (with isoprenaline if needed) after the first substrate has been eliminated, to unmask a second tachycardia. This caveat applies to every manoeuvre: they concern the tachycardia at hand, not all of the patient's substrates.
ep-man-014.aRetenir: V-A-V response: the tachycardia under study is not AT, but a coexisting AT remains possible; re-induce after ablation.

ep-man-015.question: Long RP tachycardia, concentric atrial activation. The AH is 120 ms during tachycardia. After termination, atrial pacing at the tachycardia cycle length gives an AH of 178 ms. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: AVRT via a septal pathway
Atypical AVNRT
Septal atrial tachycardia
Focal junctional tachycardia
commentaires: Incorrect: in AVRT, the AH during tachycardia reflects true antegrade nodal conduction; the ΔAH is usually < 20 ms.
Correct: ΔAH = 178 − 120 = 58 ms, above 40 ms: an AVNRT profile.
Incorrect: in AT, the atrium activates the AV node as it does during atrial pacing; the ΔAH is minimal (< 10 ms).
Incorrect: ΔAH is not a criterion for junctional tachycardia, which is distinguished by atrial pacing (A-H-H-A response) or PACs.
ep-man-015.explication: The ΔAH compares the AH during atrial pacing at the tachycardia cycle length with the AH during tachycardia. In AT or AVRT, the His is activated in series from the atrium in both situations: the ΔAH is small (< 10 ms for AT, < 20 ms for a septal pathway). In AVNRT, the atrium and His are activated in parallel from the circuit: the AH measured during tachycardia is "shortened" and does not reflect true antegrade conduction, whereas during atrial pacing the impulse has to travel through the slow pathway in series. A ΔAH > 40 ms therefore points to AVNRT. This manoeuvre is useful when ventricular pacing does not discriminate between atypical AVNRT and a septal pathway.
ep-man-015.aRetenir: ΔAH (atrial pacing at the tachycardia cycle length − tachycardia) > 40 ms: AVNRT; < 20 ms: septal pathway; < 10 ms: AT.

ep-man-016.question: Narrow-QRS tachycardia, cycle length 400 ms, central atrial activation; ventricular pacing does not accelerate the atria. You pace the atrium at 380 ms from the high RA, the CS ostium and then the distal CS. VA of the first return beat: 150, 118 and 172 ms (tachycardia VA: 150 ms). Conclusion?
options: Atypical AVNRT, because the VA is linked to ventricular activation
AVRT via a slowly conducting septal pathway
None, because only one site should have been used
Atrial tachycardia, because the return VA varies with the site
commentaires: Incorrect: in AVNRT, the first return A depends on the V ("linked" VA) and remains stable whatever the pacing site.
Incorrect: AVRT is already excluded by ventricular dissociation; moreover, its VA would also be linked.
Incorrect: it is precisely atrial pacing from several sites ("differential" pacing) that strengthens the value of the criterion.
Correct: a 54 ms difference between sites (> 14 ms) shows that the first return A depends on the distance from the focus, not on the V: an AT profile.
ep-man-016.explication: After atrial pacing 10–40 ms faster than the tachycardia, the VA of the first return beat is measured. In AVNRT (and AVRT), atrial activation is mechanistically linked to ventricular activation: the return VA remains within 10 ms of the tachycardia VA ("VA linking"). In AT, the first return A depends on the distance between the pacing site and the focus: it varies with the site. Maruyama et al. proposed pacing from two or three sites (right atrial appendage, CS ostium, distal CS): a difference in return VA > 14 ms points to septal AT. Linking is a strong argument but not proof: the return VA in AVNRT sometimes varies by more than 10 ms, and coincidental linking is possible in AT.
ep-man-016.aRetenir: Atrial pacing: stable return VA (< 10 ms difference) = AVNRT/AVRT; VA varying with the site (> 14 ms) = AT.

ep-man-017.question: Young adult, narrow-QRS tachycardia, cycle length 480 ms, simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. Atrial pacing at 450 ms: the ventricles follow. On cessation of pacing the sequence is: last paced A, His, His, then A. What is the mechanism?
options: Focal junctional tachycardia
Typical AVNRT
Septal atrial tachycardia
AVRT via a septal pathway
commentaires: Correct: an A-H-H-A response indicates a junctional focus that generates a new His before any atrial activation.
Incorrect: in AVNRT, the last paced A conducts down the slow pathway (long AH) and returns up the fast pathway: A-H-A response.
Incorrect: AT would resume with an A arising from the focus, not with two consecutive His deflections.
Incorrect: in AVRT the circuit returns to the atrium via the pathway after each V: A-H-A response.
ep-man-017.explication: Focal junctional tachycardia and typical AVNRT both have a very short VA and a V-A-V response to ventricular pacing. Atrial pacing distinguishes them (Fan et al.). In AVNRT, the last paced A conducts over the slow pathway with a long AH (PR often longer than RR), then the impulse returns up the fast pathway: A-H-A response. In junctional tachycardia, the last paced A produces a His, then the focus fires and produces a new His before the atrium: A-H-H-A response. Pitfall: if dual AV nodal physiology coexists with the junctional focus, an echo via the fast pathway may mimic an A-H-A response. Accelerated junctional rhythm in adults is seen, for example, after ablation or during isoprenaline infusion.
ep-man-017.aRetenir: Atrial pacing during a short-VA tachycardia: A-H-A = AVNRT; A-H-H-A = junctional tachycardia.

ep-man-018.question: Very short VA tachycardia: typical AVNRT or focal junctional tachycardia? You deliver premature atrial contractions (PACs) at various coupling intervals. Which interpretations are correct? (multiple answers)
options: Late PAC (His refractory) delaying the next His: AVNRT
Late PAC with no effect on the next His: definitive proof of junctional tachycardia
Early PAC advancing the immediate His, tachycardia then continuing: junctional tachycardia
Early PAC advancing the immediate His, tachycardia then terminating: junctional tachycardia
Late PAC (His refractory) advancing the next His: AVNRT, unless dual pathways coexist with a junctional focus
commentaires: Correct: the PAC penetrates the slow pathway while the fast pathway is refractory; decremental slowing delays the next His, a response specific to AVNRT.
Incorrect: no effect is expected in junctional tachycardia, but may be seen in AVNRT if the PAC fails to reach the circuit; it is not proof.
Correct: the early PAC conducts over the fast pathway and advances the His, then the junctional focus resumes; in AVNRT, the refractory fast pathway would interrupt the circuit.
Incorrect: termination is possible with either mechanism; only continuation points to junctional tachycardia.
Correct: advancement of the His by a late PAC points to AVNRT, but a junctional focus with dual pathways may produce an echo via the slow pathway.
ep-man-018.explication: Padanilam et al. showed the value of PACs in distinguishing AVNRT from junctional tachycardia. A late PAC, delivered when the junction is refractory, cannot reach a junctional focus: the paced wavefront collides with the focus's retrograde wavefront in the AV node. In AVNRT, by contrast, it can penetrate the slow pathway and advance, delay or terminate the tachycardia; delay is the most specific response. An early PAC, delivered before the His, can advance the immediate His via the fast pathway. If the tachycardia continues, it is junctional tachycardia, because in AVNRT the now-refractory fast pathway can no longer serve as the retrograde limb. The main pitfall is a junctional focus combined with dual AV nodal physiology ("dual response").
ep-man-018.aRetenir: Late PAC that modifies the next His (especially delay) = AVNRT; early PAC that advances the His with the tachycardia continuing = junctional tachycardia.

ep-man-019.question: Para-Hisian pacing in sinus rhythm. With both His + ventricular capture and ventricular capture alone, the stimulus-to-A interval (A measured at the proximal CS) remains 50 ms, with an identical atrial sequence. How should this result be interpreted?
options: Probable direct atrial capture, invalidating the manoeuvre
Extranodal response: septal accessory pathway
Nodal response via the slow pathway
Mixed retrograde conduction, both nodal and accessory
commentaires: Correct: a stimulus-to-A interval < 60 ms at the proximal CS almost always indicates direct atrial capture, which invalidates the manoeuvre.
Incorrect: such a short stimulus-to-A interval should first raise suspicion of atrial capture, which mimics an extranodal response.
Incorrect: a nodal response would show a longer stimulus-to-A interval on loss of His capture.
Incorrect: a mixed response is usually accompanied by a change in atrial sequence.
ep-man-019.explication: Para-Hisian pacing compares the stimulus-to-A interval with and without His capture: an unchanged stimulus-to-A suggests a septal accessory pathway. However, the catheter lies close to the annulus and may capture the atrium directly, which also produces a short, fixed stimulus-to-A interval that is independent of His capture. According to Obeyesekere et al., a stimulus-to-A < 60 ms at the proximal CS (or < 70 ms at the high RA) almost always indicates atrial capture; above 90 ms (proximal CS) or 100 ms (high RA), it is very unlikely. If in doubt, the catheter is moved towards the apex: loss of atrial capture then lengthens the stimulus-to-A interval by more than 20 ms. Atrial capture may also mask a genuine septal pathway.
ep-man-019.aRetenir: Para-Hisian pacing: a stimulus-to-A interval < 60 ms at the proximal CS suggests direct atrial capture, not an accessory pathway.

ep-man-020.question: During para-Hisian pacing, the stimulus-to-A interval lengthens on loss of His capture, with a constant HA and an unchanged atrial sequence. Which situations can produce this "nodal" pattern despite the presence of an accessory pathway? (multiple answers)
options: Left lateral pathway far from the pacing site
Rapidly conducting para-Hisian pathway
Slowly or decrementally conducting accessory pathway
Purely nodal retrograde conduction, with no pathway
commentaires: Correct: the pathway is too far away; the atrium is fully activated via the AV node before the wavefront reaches the pathway, with or without His capture.
Incorrect: this is the situation that gives the clearest extranodal response (unchanged stimulus-to-A, shortened HA).
Correct: if the pathway conducts more slowly than the AV node, the atrium is activated via the node and the pathway remains concealed.
Incorrect: this is a true nodal response, not a false negative, as there is no pathway.
ep-man-020.explication: Para-Hisian pacing (Hirao) is reliable for septal and right-sided pathways. A nodal response (stimulus-to-A lengthening by as much as the stimulus-to-His, constant HA, unchanged sequence) may nevertheless conceal a pathway. This occurs with a left lateral pathway that is too far away, where the atrium is activated via the AV node before the pathway is reached; eccentric activation is then better seen during RV apical pacing. It also occurs with a slow or decremental pathway that conducts more slowly than the AV node. Other pitfalls: loss of capture of the proximal left bundle alone (wider QRS without true loss of His capture), fasciculoventricular connection, atrial capture. Finally, demonstrating a pathway does not prove that it participates in the tachycardia.
ep-man-020.aRetenir: "Nodal" para-Hisian response: do not conclude that there is no pathway if it could be a distant left-sided or slow/decremental pathway.

ep-man-021.question: Patient with documented tachycardia and a baseline ECG without pre-excitation; no sustained tachycardia is inducible. Ventricular pacing at the same cycle length, stimulus-to-A measured at the high RA: 150 ms from the RV apex, 128 ms from the posterobasal RV, with no atrial capture. What do you conclude?
options: Purely nodal retrograde conduction, with no pathway
Retrograde conduction over the slow pathway
A probable (posterior) septal accessory pathway
A result that cannot be interpreted without tachycardia
commentaires: Incorrect: with purely nodal conduction, the apex is closer to the entry into the Purkinje network; the VA would be longer from the base (negative index).
Incorrect: conduction over the slow pathway would lengthen the VA, with no shortening at the base.
Correct: the VA index (apex − base) is +22 ms, above 10 ms: in favour of a septal pathway.
Incorrect: this manoeuvre is useful precisely in sinus rhythm, when no sustained tachycardia can be induced.
ep-man-021.explication: The apex/base comparison (Martinez-Alday) is based on the same principle as para-Hisian pacing. With nodal retrograde conduction, the apex is electrically closer to the His (apical entry into the Purkinje network): the VA is shorter from the apex than from the base. With a posteroseptal pathway, by contrast, pacing the base, close to the pathway insertion, shortens the VA. A VA index (apical VA − basal VA) > 10 ms had 100% sensitivity and specificity in this small study. However, a few patients without a pathway had an index of 0 to +5 ms: caution is needed with borderline values. Atrial capture at the base must be avoided; the manoeuvre is poor at detecting slowly conducting pathways.
ep-man-021.aRetenir: VA index (apex − base) > 10 ms = septal pathway; nodal conduction = longer VA from the base.
